CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3

CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3 · APRIL

Drawing prisms and pyramids

How do you get a solid onto paper? As a net to cut out and fold, as an oblique drawing that looks three-dimensional, or as a two-view drawing like in a building plan, from the front and from above. You get to know all three representations. And you find out how long a sloping edge really is, even though it looks too short in every drawing.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS3 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • recognise, name and compare prisms and pyramids
  • draw nets and fold solids from them
  • draw prisms and pyramids as an oblique drawing
  • draw and read two-view drawings with top view, front view and projection lines
  • construct the true length of a line segment and the true shape of a face
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

How many edges does a cuboid have?

12: four at the bottom, four at the top, four vertical.

How many faces does a cube have?

6

A cuboid is 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm long. What is its volume?

$2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24$ cm³

A right angle is halved. How big is each half?

45°

EXPLORATIONSTO GET STARTED · IN GROUPS
COLLECTING SOLIDS

Collect boxes, packaging and objects: a pencil, a tent, a roof, a bar of chocolate in its box.

  • Sort them: which have two equal, parallel faces? Which come together in a point at the top?
→ Unit 1
NETS OF A CUBE

A cube can be cut open and laid flat in different ways.

  • Draw as many different nets of a cube as you can on squared paper. Rotated and reflected ones do not count as new.
  • How many do you find?
→ Unit 1
FROM THE FRONT, FROM ABOVE

Put an object on the table, for example a box with a pen on top of it.

  • Draw what it looks like exactly from the front, and below that what it looks like exactly from above.
  • Can the group next to you guess the object from your two pictures?

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Nets and oblique drawings

A pencil has two equal hexagons as its ends and nothing but rectangles in between: a prism. A tent with a square floor comes together in a point at the top: a pyramid. Both solids are named after their base.

KEY POINT · PRISMS, PYRAMIDS, NETS, OBLIQUE DRAWINGS

Prism: The base and the top face are congruent, parallel polygons. In a right prism the lateral faces are rectangles. Cuboids and cubes are prisms.

Pyramid: The base is a polygon; the lateral faces are triangles with a common apex $S$. The height $h$ is the distance of the apex from the base.

Net: All the faces of the solid joined together in the plane so that the solid can be folded from it.

Oblique drawing: Width and height true to size. Edges that go backwards at $45^\circ$ and shortened to half. Hidden edges dashed.

Counting: A prism with an $n$-gon as its base has $2n$ vertices, $3n$ edges and $n + 2$ faces.

Right pyramid: The apex lies exactly above the centre of the base. In this book all pyramids are right pyramids.

INTERACTIVE · FROM NET TO SOLID

Choose a solid and fold it with the slider or the button. Drag the picture to turn the solid.

INTERACTIVE · THE OBLIQUE DRAWING

Choose a solid and change the measurements. Look at the edges going backwards: they slope and are half as long.

EXAMPLE 1 · A CUBOID IN OBLIQUE DRAWING

Draw the oblique drawing of a cuboid with $a = 4$ cm (width), $b = 3$ cm (depth) and $c = 2$ cm (height).

Draw the front face as a rectangle 4 cm × 2 cm. From each corner draw an edge going backwards: at $45^\circ$, but only $3 \div 2 = 1.5$ cm long.

Join the back corners. The three edges at the bottom back left corner are hidden: dashed.

EXAMPLE 2 · THE NET OF A PYRAMID

Draw the net of a square-based pyramid with $a = 3$ cm. The lateral triangles are isosceles and 4 cm high.

Draw the square with side length 3 cm. On each side erect an isosceles triangle 4 cm high: the apex lies 4 cm above the midpoint of the side.

The net looks like a star with four points.

EXERCISES

Count the vertices, edges and faces: a) hexagonal prism   b) pentagonal pyramid   c) triangular prism

a) 12, 18, 8   b) 6, 10, 6   c) 6, 9, 5

Draw the oblique drawing of a cube with edge length 4 cm and that of a triangular prism with an equilateral triangle (3 cm) as its base and a height of 5 cm.

Cube: front face 4 cm × 4 cm, depth edges 2 cm at 45°. Prism: stand it on the triangle. The edge of the triangle at the front is 3 cm long; the tip of the triangle lies at the back and appears shortened.

Draw two different nets of a cuboid with edge lengths 3 cm, 2 cm and 1 cm. Cut one out and fold it.

For example: four lateral faces in a row (3, 2, 3, 2 cm wide, 1 cm high) and a rectangle 3 cm × 2 cm above and below one of the long faces.

How many different nets of a cube are there? Find at least six. Rotated and reflected nets do not count as new.

There are exactly 11 nets of a cube. Six of them have four squares in a row, plus one square above and one below.

A prism and a pyramid both have an $n$-gon as their base. Give the number of vertices, edges and faces for each. Check with $n = 4$.

Prism: $2n$ vertices, $3n$ edges, $n + 2$ faces. Pyramid: $n + 1$ vertices, $2n$ edges, $n + 1$ faces. For $n = 4$: cuboid 8, 12, 6 and square-based pyramid 5, 8, 5.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many edges does a triangular prism have?

$3 \cdot 3 = 9$

How many faces does a square-based pyramid have?

A square and four triangles: 5.

An edge going backwards is 6 cm long. How long do you draw it in the oblique drawing?

Half as long: 3 cm.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2The two-view drawing

Anyone building a house needs exact measurements. An oblique drawing looks nice, but you cannot measure every length in it. That is why architects and engineers draw the solid from the front and from above, exactly perpendicular, and put the two pictures one below the other.

KEY POINT · THE TWO-VIEW DRAWING

The solid stands in front of two planes that are perpendicular to each other. The view from the front is called the front view, the view from above the top view (plan).

The two planes meet in the folding line $x_{12}$. The front view is above it, the top view below it.

Points that belong together lie on a projection line perpendicular to the folding line. A point $P$ is called $P'$ in the top view and $P''$ in the front view.

The distance of $P''$ from the folding line is the height of $P$. Hidden edges are dashed.

Perpendicular from the front: Edges that point straight backwards appear as a point in the front view.

On the computer: Many programs for solids show the three views from the front, from above and from the side next to each other.

INTERACTIVE · FRONT VIEW AND TOP VIEW

Choose different solids. Follow the dotted projection lines from the bottom to the top.

THREE REPRESENTATIONS COMPARED
NetOblique drawingTwo-view drawing
Advantageall faces true to size, for making modelseasy to picture, you recognise the solid at onceexact measurements, as in a building plan
Disadvantagethe solid is hard to recognisedepths and angles distortedtakes practice to read
EXAMPLE 3 · A PYRAMID IN A TWO-VIEW DRAWING

Draw the two-view drawing of a square-based pyramid with $a = 4$ cm and $h = 5$ cm standing on the plane of the top view.

Top view: a square with side length 4 cm. The apex $S'$ lies at the centre; the lateral edges appear as diagonals.

Front view: a triangle with a 4 cm base on the folding line and a height of 5 cm, $S''$ exactly above $S'$.

EXAMPLE 4 · READING THE VIEWS

The front view is a rectangle, the top view an equilateral triangle. Which solid is it?

From above a triangle: the base and the top face are triangles. From the front a rectangle: the sides are vertical.

A triangular prism standing on its base.

EXERCISES

Draw the two-view drawing of a cuboid 5 cm wide, 3 cm deep and 2 cm high. Label the vertices.

Top view: rectangle 5 cm × 3 cm. Front view: rectangle 5 cm × 2 cm. The vertical edges of the top view go upwards as projection lines.

Which solid is it? a) front view a triangle, top view a square with diagonals   b) front view and top view rectangles   c) front view a rectangle, top view a hexagon

a) square-based pyramid   b) cuboid   c) hexagonal prism

Draw the two-view drawing of a regular hexagonal prism with a base edge of 2 cm and a height of 4 cm. Construct the hexagon with compasses.

Top view: regular hexagon with side length 2 cm (mark off the radius 2 cm six times on the circle). Front view: rectangle 4 cm wide and 4 cm high with two vertical edges inside.

Which representation fits best? a) a cut-out sheet for a model house   b) a picture in a furniture catalogue   c) a plan for the workshop

a) net   b) oblique drawing   c) two-view drawing

A solid has a square as its front view and a square as its top view. Must it be a cube?

No. A wedge, i.e. a triangular prism lying down with its triangles on the left and right, looks square from the front and from above, but triangular from the side. Two views do not always determine a solid.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the view from above called?

The top view.

A point lies 3 cm above the plane of the top view. How far is $P''$ from the folding line?

3 cm, exactly its height.

A vertical edge is 5 cm long. How long does it appear in the front view?

It is parallel to the plane of the front view: 5 cm.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3True length and true shape

In the two-view drawing of the pyramid ($a = 4$ cm, $h = 5$ cm) measure the lateral edge $\overline{S''B''}$: about 5.4 cm. In the top view $\overline{S'B'}$ is only about 2.8 cm long. But a model shows: the edge is about 5.7 cm long. It slopes in space and appears shortened in both views.

KEY POINT · TRUE LENGTH AND TRUE SHAPE

A line segment appears in a view in its true length if it lies parallel to the plane of this view. Otherwise it appears shorter.

Construction for a lateral edge $\overline{SB}$ of a pyramid:

  1. In the top view, turn $B'$ on an arc about $S'$ until $\overline{S'B_0'}$ is parallel to the folding line.
  2. The projection line through $B_0'$ meets the bottom line of the front view at $B_0''$.
  3. $\overline{S''B_0''}$ is the true length of the edge.

You construct the true shape of a face from the true lengths of its sides, for example a lateral triangle from $a$ and twice $\overline{SB}$.

Why turn it? When you turn it about the vertical axis through $S$, neither the length of the edge nor its height changes. Only its direction changes, until it lies parallel to the plane of the front view.

INTERACTIVE · THE TRUE LENGTH OF A LATERAL EDGE

Blue: the edge in both views. Red: the turn in the top view. Yellow: the true length in the front view. Change $a$ and $h$.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE LATERAL EDGE

Construct the true length of a lateral edge of the pyramid with $a = 4$ cm and $h = 5$ cm.

Draw the two-view drawing. Turn $B'$ about $S'$ onto the parallel to the folding line through $S'$. The projection line leads to $B_0''$ on the bottom line of the front view.

You measure $\overline{S''B_0''} \approx 5.7$ cm.

EXAMPLE 6 · THE LATERAL FACE

Construct the true shape of a lateral face of this pyramid and measure its height.

The lateral face is an isosceles triangle with a 4 cm base and two legs of 5.7 cm. Construct it from three sides.

You measure the height of the lateral face: about 5.4 cm.

EXERCISES

A cuboid stands on the plane of the top view with one lateral face parallel to the plane of the front view. Which edges appear in the front view in their true length, and which as a point?

The horizontal edges from left to right and the vertical edges appear in their true length. The edges going backwards appear as points.

Construct the true length of a lateral edge of a square-based pyramid with $a = 3$ cm and $h = 4$ cm. Measure it.

You measure about 4.5 cm.

Construct the true shape of a lateral face of this pyramid. How high is the lateral triangle?

Triangle from 3 cm, 4.5 cm and 4.5 cm. Its height measures about 4.3 cm.

A cuboid is 4 cm wide, 3 cm deep and 2 cm high. Construct the true length of its space diagonal. Hint: you see the diagonal of the base in its true length in the top view.

In the top view the diagonal of the base measures 5 cm. Draw a right-angled triangle with the shorter sides 5 cm and 2 cm. Its longest side is the space diagonal: about 5.4 cm.

Explain why, for a square-based pyramid whose base edges are parallel to the planes of the views, no lateral edge appears in its true length in the top view or the front view.

Every lateral edge rises, so it is not parallel to the plane of the top view. And it points diagonally forwards or backwards, so it is not parallel to the plane of the front view either. That is why you have to turn it.

TEST YOURSELF!

When does a line segment appear in the front view in its true length?

Only when parallel. Perpendicular to the plane it appears as a point.

A line segment 4 cm long is perpendicular to the plane of the top view. How long does it appear in the top view?

As a point: 0 cm.

A square-based pyramid has $a = 6$ cm. How long does a base edge appear in the top view?

It lies in the plane of the top view: 6 cm.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A prism has 7 faces. What base does it have? How many vertices and edges?

$n + 2 = 7$, so $n = 5$: a pentagonal prism with 10 vertices and 15 edges.

Connecting with chapter 1.3: The true shape of a lateral face is a triangle construction. Which case (SSS, SAS, ASA) is it? Write a description of the construction.

Case SSS: draw the base edge $a$, circles round both end points with the true length of the lateral edge; their point of intersection is the apex.

If you cut the top off a square-based pyramid horizontally, you get a frustum of a pyramid. Draw its oblique drawing for a base edge of 4 cm, a top edge of 2 cm and a height of 3 cm. How many vertices, edges and faces does it have?

8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 faces: two squares and four trapeziums. More on this in chapter 3.2.

A house consists of a cuboid (8 m wide, 6 m deep, 5 m high) with a gable roof: the ridge is 3 m above the eaves and runs from left to right. Draw the top view and the front view to the scale 1 : 100.

Top view: rectangle 8 cm × 6 cm with the ridge as a line in the middle. Front view: rectangle 8 cm × 5 cm for the walls, on top a rectangle 8 cm × 3 cm for the front roof surface. Its upper edge is the ridge; the back roof surface is hidden.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Gaspard Monge and the secret art of drawing

As a young man Gaspard Monge (1746 to 1818) worked at a military school in Mézières in France. Fortresses were planned there, and that was laborious: people calculated for a long time to find out which wall could be seen from where. Monge found a quicker way. He drew the building from the front and from above and folded both pictures into one plane, exactly as in this chapter.

For years his method was regarded as a military secret. Only in 1799 did his book Géométrie descriptive, “descriptive geometry”, appear, based on lectures at the École Normale in Paris. To this day engineers and architects draw by Monge’s rules.

Source: G. Monge, Géométrie descriptive, Paris, Baudouin, An VII (1799).

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

PRISM AND PYRAMID

Prism: two equal parallel polygons · pyramid: polygon and apex

$n$-sided prism: $2n$, $3n$, $n + 2$

NET

All faces joined together in the plane, can be folded

Cube: 11 nets

OBLIQUE DRAWING

Depth at $45^\circ$ and halved, hidden edges dashed

Depth 6 cm → 3 cm

TWO-VIEW DRAWING

Front view above, top view below, folding line $x_{12}$, projection lines

$P'$ in the top view, $P''$ in the front view

TRUE LENGTH

Unshortened only when parallel to the plane of the view, otherwise turn it

Pyramid 4 cm, 5 cm: edge ≈ 5.7 cm
